stem: A septic patient has platelets 40 × 10⁹/L, markedly elevated D-dimer, PT prolonged by 7 seconds and fibrinogen 0.9 g/L. What is the ISTH overt DIC score?
explanation: ISTH scoring: platelets below 50 = 2 points; strong D-dimer increase = 3; PT prolonged by ≥6 seconds = 2; fibrinogen below 1 g/L = 1. Total 8. A score of 5 or more is compatible with overt DIC.
referenceText: Taylor et al. 2001 (ISTH overt DIC score) [206]

stem: A patient with sepsis-associated DIC has platelets 35 × 10⁹/L and fibrinogen 1.2 g/L but no bleeding and no planned procedure. What is the most appropriate management?

options.C: Treat the sepsis and avoid prophylactic platelet or cryoprecipitate transfusion
options.D: Give cryoprecipitate to normalise fibrinogen above 2 g/L before any further decline

explanation: DIC management centres on treating the cause. Blood components are given for bleeding or before invasive procedures (platelets to keep above 50 × 10⁹/L when bleeding; fibrinogen replacement for levels below 1.5 g/L with bleeding). Antifibrinolytics are generally avoided in sepsis-associated DIC because fibrinolysis is already suppressed.
referenceText: Taylor et al. 2001 (ISTH overt DIC score) [206]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: On day 7 of UFH prophylaxis after surgery, a patient's platelet count falls from 260 to 95 × 10⁹/L and a new DVT is found. No other cause is apparent. What is the 4Ts score and probability of HIT?

options.D: 6; low probability because surgery explains thrombocytopenia

explanation: 4Ts: thrombocytopenia (fall >50% with nadir ≥20) = 2; timing (onset days 5–10) = 2; thrombosis (new) = 2; other causes (none apparent) = 2; total 8. Scores of 6–8 indicate high probability, 4–5 intermediate and 0–3 low (where HIT can be excluded without testing).
referenceText: Cuker et al. 2018 (ASH heparin-induced thrombocytopenia) [43]

stem: A patient with suspected HIT (4Ts score 7) has normal liver function and creatinine clearance of 25 mL/min. What is the recommended management while awaiting antibody results?

options.A: Stop all heparin and start a non-heparin anticoagulant (e.g. argatroban)
options.C: Stop heparin and give no anticoagulant at all until the laboratory assay result returns

explanation: In intermediate or high-probability HIT, ASH recommends stopping all heparin and starting a non-heparin anticoagulant (argatroban, bivalirudin, fondaparinux or a DOAC), because the thrombosis risk is high even without overt thrombosis. Argatroban is hepatically cleared, suitable in renal impairment. Warfarin should be delayed until platelets recover.
referenceText: Cuker et al. 2018 (ASH heparin-induced thrombocytopenia) [43]

stem: In a patient with acute HIT without bleeding, why are prophylactic platelet transfusions avoided?

options.A: They may fuel thrombosis, and severe bleeding is uncommon in HIT
options.D: Platelets are destroyed instantly and so have no clinical effect
options.E: Platelet transfusion causes TRALI in all patients

explanation: HIT is a prothrombotic disorder; bleeding is rare despite thrombocytopenia. ASH suggests against routine platelet transfusion in patients at average bleeding risk, reserving transfusion for active bleeding or high-risk procedures.
referenceText: Cuker et al. 2018 (ASH heparin-induced thrombocytopenia) [43]

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with confusion, fever, platelets 12 × 10⁹/L, schistocytes, raised LDH, undetectable haptoglobin and creatinine 110 µmol/L. Which test confirms the diagnosis?
explanation: TTP is caused by severe ADAMTS13 deficiency (activity below 10%), usually autoimmune. Coagulation tests are typically normal and the direct antiglobulin test negative. The PLASMIC score helps estimate probability before ADAMTS13 results are available.
referenceText: Zheng et al. 2020 (ISTH TTP treatment) [247]; Bendapudi et al. 2017 (PLASMIC score) [16]

stem: A patient with suspected immune TTP has a high PLASMIC score. What is the recommended initial therapy?

options.A: Platelet transfusion to above 50 × 10⁹/L before central line insertion for plasma exchange
options.E: Urgent plasma exchange with corticosteroids; consider caplacizumab and rituximab

explanation: ISTH recommends plasma exchange plus corticosteroids for immune TTP; caplacizumab (anti-von Willebrand factor nanobody) and rituximab are suggested. Platelet transfusion should be avoided unless life-threatening bleeding because it may worsen microthrombosis. Plasma infusion is a temporary measure if exchange is delayed.
referenceText: Zheng et al. 2020 (ISTH TTP treatment) [247]

stem: A patient with microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and AKI has ADAMTS13 activity of 60% and no diarrhoeal illness. Infection, drugs and malignancy are excluded. What is the most appropriate targeted therapy?

options.C: Antibiotics directed against Shiga toxin-producing E. coli

explanation: Complement-mediated (atypical) HUS results from dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway. ADAMTS13 above 10% excludes TTP. C5 inhibitors are the treatment of choice; meningococcal vaccination and prophylaxis are required.
referenceText: Zheng et al. 2020 (ISTH TTP treatment) [247]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: What did the PROPPR trial show when comparing a 1:1:1 ratio of plasma, platelets and red cells with 1:1:2 in severe trauma?

options.A: No difference in 24-hour or 30-day mortality, but better haemostasis and fewer exsanguination deaths
options.D: 1:1:1 caused more ARDS, multiorgan failure, transfusion reactions and 30-day deaths from late sepsis

explanation: PROPPR randomised 680 trauma patients; mortality was not significantly different overall, but the 1:1:1 group had more haemostasis and fewer early exsanguination deaths, without increased complications. High-ratio transfusion is widely used in major haemorrhage protocols.
referenceText: Holcomb et al. 2015 (PROPPR) [93]; Rossaint et al. 2023 (European trauma bleeding guideline, 6th ed.) [184]

stem: A bleeding trauma patient's ROTEM shows a FIBTEM maximum clot firmness of 5 mm (low) with normal EXTEM clotting time. What is the most appropriate therapy?

options.C: Fresh frozen plasma alone at 15–20 mL/kg

explanation: FIBTEM assesses fibrin polymerisation with platelets inhibited; a low maximum clot firmness indicates fibrinogen deficiency. European trauma guidelines recommend fibrinogen replacement when FIBTEM MCF is below about 7 mm or plasma fibrinogen is below 1.5 g/L. A low EXTEM MCF with normal FIBTEM suggests platelet deficiency.
referenceText: Rossaint et al. 2023 (European trauma bleeding guideline, 6th ed.) [184]

stem: According to the European trauma guideline, at what plasma fibrinogen level should fibrinogen be replaced in a bleeding trauma patient?
explanation: The sixth edition recommends treatment with fibrinogen concentrate or cryoprecipitate if significant bleeding is accompanied by viscoelastic signs of a functional fibrinogen deficit or plasma fibrinogen of 1.5 g/L or less. Fibrinogen is the first factor to fall critically in massive haemorrhage.
referenceText: Rossaint et al. 2023 (European trauma bleeding guideline, 6th ed.) [184]

stem: What is the recommended regimen and timing of tranexamic acid in trauma with significant haemorrhage?

options.A: 1 g given only if bleeding persists after 6 hours
options.B: 1 g over 10 minutes then 1 g over 8 hours, given within 3 hours of injury
options.C: 2 g bolus at any time after injury
options.D: Given only after viscoelastic evidence of hyperfibrinolysis beyond 3 hours

explanation: CRASH-2 showed reduced death from bleeding when tranexamic acid was started within 3 hours; late treatment (after 3 hours) was associated with increased bleeding deaths. European guidelines recommend early administration, ideally en route to hospital.
referenceText: CRASH-2 Collaborators 2010 [41]; Rossaint et al. 2023 (European trauma bleeding guideline, 6th ed.) [184]

stem: What did the MINT trial suggest about transfusion thresholds in patients with acute myocardial infarction and anaemia?

options.A: Liberal transfusion (<10 g/dL) may reduce death or reinfarction, though not statistically significant
options.B: Both strategies increased heart failure equally
options.D: Transfusion is contraindicated in acute myocardial infarction because of the risks of thrombosis and overload

explanation: MINT randomised 3504 patients with MI and haemoglobin below 10 g/dL. The primary outcome of death or recurrent MI at 30 days was 16.9% (restrictive) vs 14.5% (liberal), not statistically significant, but the results suggest possible harm from restrictive thresholds in MI. TRICC supported restrictive thresholds in general ICU patients.
referenceText: Carson et al. 2023 (MINT) [32]; Hébert et al. 1999 (TRICC) [99]

stem: Minutes after starting a red cell transfusion, a patient develops fever, back pain, hypotension and haemoglobinuria. What is the first action?

options.A: Give furosemide and continue the transfusion
options.B: Give a second unit to correct anaemia
options.C: Slow the transfusion rate and give paracetamol, then reassess the patient in 30 minutes
options.E: Stop the transfusion, keep IV access with saline, and check patient and unit identity

explanation: Acute haemolytic transfusion reactions usually result from ABO incompatibility due to identification errors. The transfusion must be stopped at once, with supportive care (fluids to maintain urine output, treatment of DIC and shock) and investigations (DAT, repeat crossmatch, haemolysis markers). The unit and paperwork should be returned to the blood bank.
referenceText: Delaney et al. 2016 (transfusion reactions) [50]

stem: An elderly patient with heart failure develops dyspnoea, hypertension, raised JVP and bilateral crackles during her third unit of red cells. BNP is markedly elevated. What is the diagnosis?
explanation: TACO presents with hydrostatic pulmonary oedema, hypertension and raised filling pressures during or within 12 hours of transfusion. Risk factors include heart failure, renal failure, positive fluid balance and age. Management includes stopping transfusion, diuretics and oxygen; slower transfusion of single units reduces risk.
referenceText: Delaney et al. 2016 (transfusion reactions) [50]

stem: A patient develops anaphylaxis within minutes of starting plasma transfusion. Investigations reveal undetectable IgA with anti-IgA antibodies. How should future transfusions be managed?

options.A: Avoid all blood products for life, including albumin
options.D: Use IgA-deficient donor products or washed cells

explanation: Severe IgA deficiency with anti-IgA antibodies can cause anaphylactic transfusion reactions. Future transfusions should use IgA-deficient plasma or washed red cells and platelets. Acute management follows anaphylaxis guidelines with IM adrenaline.
referenceText: Delaney et al. 2016 (transfusion reactions) [50]; Cardona et al. 2020 (WAO anaphylaxis guidance) [30]

stem: A patient develops high fever, rigors and septic shock within minutes of a platelet transfusion. Which mechanism is most likely?

options.A: Transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease from donor lymphocytes
options.D: Bacterial contamination; platelets are stored at room temperature

explanation: Platelets are stored at 20–24 °C, which promotes bacterial growth, making them the component most often associated with transfusion-transmitted sepsis. The transfusion should be stopped, cultures taken from the patient and unit, and broad-spectrum antibiotics started.
referenceText: Delaney et al. 2016 (transfusion reactions) [50]

stem: Which patients require irradiated cellular blood components to prevent transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease?

options.C: HSCT recipients, patients on purine analogues, and HLA-matched or related-donor recipients
options.E: Patients with sickle cell disease or thalassaemia only, during exchange transfusion programmes

explanation: TA-GVHD is almost universally fatal and occurs when donor lymphocytes engraft in an immunocompromised or HLA-similar recipient. Irradiation inactivates lymphocytes. Indications include congenital immunodeficiency, stem cell transplantation, purine analogue therapy (e.g. fludarabine), Hodgkin lymphoma and directed donations from relatives.
referenceText: Delaney et al. 2016 (transfusion reactions) [50]

stem: According to the AABB guideline, what platelet count threshold is suggested for prophylactic transfusion before central venous catheter placement?
explanation: AABB suggests prophylactic platelet transfusion at counts below 10 × 10⁹/L in hospitalised patients with therapy-induced hypoproliferative thrombocytopenia, below 20 × 10⁹/L for elective central venous catheter placement, and below 50 × 10⁹/L for elective lumbar puncture and major non-neuraxial surgery. Ultrasound guidance reduces bleeding risk.
referenceText: Kaufman et al. 2015 (AABB platelet transfusion) [111]

stem: A non-bleeding ICU patient with INR 1.7 needs an ultrasound-guided central line. What is the recommended approach?

options.A: Give vitamin K and delay the procedure for 48 hours until the INR normalises
options.D: Proceed without prophylactic plasma; mild INR rise does not predict bleeding

explanation: Mildly elevated INR (up to about 1.5–2) does not predict bleeding with ultrasound-guided procedures, and FFP rarely corrects mild INR prolongation while exposing patients to TACO and TRALI. Plasma should be reserved for bleeding or high-risk procedures with significant coagulopathy.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]; Rossaint et al. 2023 (European trauma bleeding guideline, 6th ed.) [184]

stem: A patient who received an IV bolus of 5000 units of unfractionated heparin 30 minutes ago develops major bleeding. What is the appropriate protamine dose?

options.B: Protamine is ineffective against unfractionated heparin when given as an IV bolus
options.C: About 50 mg slowly (1 mg per 100 units of recent heparin, maximum 50 mg)

explanation: Protamine neutralises UFH at about 1 mg per 100 units of heparin remaining in the circulation (heparin half-life about 60–90 minutes), up to 50 mg per dose. Rapid administration causes hypotension, bradycardia and anaphylactoid reactions. Protamine only partially reverses LMWH.
referenceText: Tomaselli et al. 2020 (ACC oral anticoagulant bleeding pathway) [214]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: A well patient has an unexpectedly low platelet count of 35 × 10⁹/L with no bleeding. The blood film shows platelet clumps. What is the next step?

options.B: Stop all anticoagulants and start argatroban for presumed heparin-induced thrombocytopenia
options.E: Repeat in a citrate tube to exclude EDTA-dependent pseudothrombocytopenia

explanation: EDTA-dependent platelet clumping causes spuriously low automated counts. A blood film showing clumps and a normal count in citrate confirm pseudothrombocytopenia, avoiding unnecessary investigations and treatment.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: Which drug is a well-recognised cause of thrombocytopenia in ICU patients receiving prolonged therapy?

options.C: Omeprazole at standard doses for 1 day

explanation: Linezolid causes dose- and duration-dependent myelosuppression, especially thrombocytopenia after 10–14 days or in renal impairment. Other ICU drugs implicated include heparin (HIT), vancomycin, beta-lactams, glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors, quinine, valproate and piperacillin.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]; Cuker et al. 2018 (ASH heparin-induced thrombocytopenia) [43]

stem: Which measure most effectively reduces transfusion requirements from anaemia in critically ill patients?

options.B: Minimising diagnostic phlebotomy (small-volume tubes, blood-conserving systems)
options.C: Daily full blood counts and coagulation screens so that anaemia is detected and treated early
options.D: Daily IV iron in all patients

explanation: Phlebotomy contributes substantially to ICU anaemia (often 40–70 mL/day). Blood conservation strategies (smaller tubes, closed sampling, avoiding routine daily tests) reduce transfusion. Erythropoietin has not consistently reduced transfusion and may increase thrombosis.
referenceText: Hébert et al. 1999 (TRICC) [99]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: A patient with sickle cell disease has new infiltrates, fever, hypoxaemia (SpO2 88% on air) and falling haemoglobin. What is the most appropriate specific treatment for severe deterioration?

options.C: Avoid transfusion, because it increases blood viscosity and worsens sickling
options.D: Hydration alone with 5 L of IV fluid
options.E: Exchange transfusion, with antibiotics, oxygen, analgesia and spirometry

explanation: Acute chest syndrome is a leading cause of death in sickle cell disease. BSH guidance recommends antibiotics (including atypical coverage), oxygen, analgesia, incentive spirometry, and simple or exchange transfusion depending on severity; exchange transfusion is used for severe or progressive hypoxaemia.
referenceText: Howard et al. 2015 (acute chest syndrome guideline) [95]

stem: A young man of Mediterranean origin develops acute haemolysis with haemoglobinuria after eating fava beans. Blood film shows bite cells and Heinz bodies. Which drug used in the ICU should be avoided in this condition?
explanation: G6PD deficiency is common in Egypt and the Mediterranean region. Oxidative stressors (fava beans, infections, primaquine, dapsone, sulfonamides, rasburicase, methylene blue) cause haemolysis. Rasburicase generates hydrogen peroxide and is contraindicated; methylene blue may worsen methaemoglobinaemia in these patients.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]; Nelson et al. 2019 (Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies) [151]

stem: A patient with newly diagnosed acute myeloid leukaemia has white cell count 220 × 10⁹/L, hypoxaemia and confusion. Which action should be avoided?

options.B: Cytoreduction with hydroxyurea and urgent induction chemotherapy
options.C: Red cell transfusion to normalise haemoglobin

explanation: Leukostasis is caused by hyperviscosity from blasts in the microcirculation (lungs, brain). Red cell transfusion increases viscosity and should be avoided or minimised. Management includes rapid cytoreduction, TLS prophylaxis and, in some cases, leukapheresis.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: A patient with persistent fever, splenomegaly, cytopenias, ferritin above 20,000 µg/L, hypertriglyceridaemia and low fibrinogen does not respond to antibiotics. Which diagnosis should be considered?
explanation: HLH is a hyperinflammatory syndrome triggered by infection (e.g. EBV), malignancy or autoimmune disease, with fever, cytopenias, very high ferritin, hypertriglyceridaemia, hypofibrinogenaemia and haemophagocytosis. The HScore estimates probability. Treatment includes corticosteroids, etoposide or anakinra and treatment of the trigger.
referenceText: Fardet et al. 2014 (HScore) [67]

stem: A critically ill patient has active GI bleeding. What VTE prophylaxis is appropriate?

options.C: No prophylaxis of any kind for the rest of the ICU stay, because bleeding risk persists long term
options.D: Intermittent pneumatic compression until bleeding risk falls, then pharmacological prophylaxis

explanation: Critically ill patients are at high VTE risk. When pharmacological prophylaxis is contraindicated by bleeding, mechanical prophylaxis (intermittent pneumatic compression) is used, with LMWH or UFH started as soon as bleeding risk falls.
referenceText: Kahn et al. 2012 (ACCP VTE prevention, non-surgical) [108]; Evans et al. 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) [65]

stem: A patient with lupus develops multiorgan thrombosis (renal, cerebral, skin) within a week, with thrombocytopenia and positive lupus anticoagulant. What is the recommended treatment?

options.D: Heparin anticoagulation, high-dose corticosteroids, and plasma exchange and/or IVIG
options.E: Platelet transfusion, and stop anticoagulation until the platelet count has recovered

explanation: Catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome causes rapid multiorgan microthrombosis with high mortality. Triple therapy with anticoagulation, glucocorticoids and plasma exchange and/or IVIG is recommended; rituximab or eculizumab may be used in refractory cases.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: A patient on warfarin has INR 9.2 with no bleeding. What is the appropriate management?

options.A: Withhold warfarin and give low-dose oral vitamin K (2–2.5 mg), monitoring INR
options.B: Give IV vitamin K 10 mg and protamine to reverse the anticoagulation immediately
options.D: Continue warfarin at the same dose

explanation: For INR above 9 without bleeding, guidance recommends holding warfarin and giving low-dose oral vitamin K, rechecking INR. Rapid reversal with PCC and IV vitamin K is reserved for major bleeding or urgent surgery.
referenceText: Tomaselli et al. 2020 (ACC oral anticoagulant bleeding pathway) [214]

stem: Why may anti-Xa levels be preferred to aPTT for monitoring unfractionated heparin in critically ill patients?

options.A: aPTT is unaffected by any patient-related factor, so it is always more accurate than anti-Xa
options.B: aPTT is altered by high factor VIII and fibrinogen, lupus anticoagulant and coagulopathy
options.C: aPTT is only used for warfarin
options.E: Anti-Xa cannot be measured in plasma

explanation: In critical illness, raised factor VIII and fibrinogen shorten the aPTT (apparent heparin resistance), while factor deficiencies and lupus anticoagulant prolong it. Anti-Xa assays measure heparin effect more directly (target typically 0.3–0.7 IU/mL for therapeutic UFH).
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]; Cuker et al. 2018 (ASH heparin-induced thrombocytopenia) [43]

stem: A patient on ECMO requires very high doses of heparin without reaching the target anti-Xa level. What may explain this?
explanation: Heparin acts by potentiating antithrombin. Acquired AT deficiency (consumption on extracorporeal circuits, sepsis, liver failure, nephrotic syndrome) causes heparin resistance. Supplementation or switching to direct thrombin inhibitors may be considered.
referenceText: Tonna et al. 2021 (ELSO VV-ECMO guideline) [215]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

topic: von Willebrand disease and uraemic bleeding
stem: A patient with uraemia and AKI has bleeding from line sites with normal platelet count and coagulation tests. Which drug improves platelet function?
explanation: Uraemia causes platelet dysfunction. Desmopressin releases von Willebrand factor and factor VIII from endothelial stores, improving platelet adhesion within an hour (tachyphylaxis after repeated doses). Dialysis, correction of anaemia, cryoprecipitate and conjugated oestrogens are other options.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]; Tomaselli et al. 2020 (ACC oral anticoagulant bleeding pathway) [214]
tags: von Willebrand disease and uraemic bleeding

stem: A competent adult Jehovah's Witness with severe anaemia from GI bleeding refuses red cell transfusion after full explanation of the risk of death. What is the appropriate response?

options.A: Ask family members to consent to transfusion on the patient's behalf, as the risk of death is high
options.B: Respect the informed refusal and use blood conservation (haemostasis, iron, EPO, minimal sampling)
options.C: Transfuse under sedation because life is at risk
options.E: Obtain a court order immediately in all cases

explanation: A competent adult may refuse any treatment, including life-saving blood, and an advance directive must be respected. Management focuses on preventing further blood loss, maximising haematopoiesis, reducing oxygen consumption and discussing which fractions or techniques (e.g. cell salvage, albumin) the patient may accept.
referenceText: Truog et al. 2008 (ACCM end-of-life care) [216]; Rossaint et al. 2023 (European trauma bleeding guideline, 6th ed.) [184]

stem: A patient develops symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage 2 hours after alteplase for ischaemic stroke. Besides stopping the infusion, which treatment is recommended?

options.B: Cryoprecipitate (or fibrinogen) plus tranexamic or aminocaproic acid
options.C: Further alteplase at half dose to complete reperfusion

explanation: Alteplase causes hypofibrinogenaemia and fibrinolysis. AHA/ASA suggest cryoprecipitate (10 units) to raise fibrinogen above 1.5–2 g/L and antifibrinolytics (tranexamic acid or aminocaproic acid), with neurosurgical consultation and BP control.
referenceText: Powers et al. 2019 (AHA/ASA acute ischaemic stroke) [168]; Tomaselli et al. 2020 (ACC oral anticoagulant bleeding pathway) [214]

stem: Which combination of factors worsens trauma-induced coagulopathy and is targeted during damage control resuscitation?
explanation: Hypothermia impairs enzyme function and platelet activity; acidosis reduces coagulation factor activity; hypocalcaemia (from citrate and shock) impairs clotting. Damage control resuscitation includes warming, permissive hypotension, early haemostatic resuscitation and calcium replacement.
referenceText: Rossaint et al. 2023 (European trauma bleeding guideline, 6th ed.) [184]; ACS Committee on Trauma 2018 (ATLS, 10th ed.) [5]

stem: Seven days after transfusion, a patient has unexplained falling haemoglobin, jaundice and a newly positive direct antiglobulin test. What is the most likely explanation?

options.A: Delayed haemolytic reaction from an anamnestic alloantibody response
options.C: Transfusion-associated circulatory overload with hepatic congestion

explanation: Delayed haemolytic reactions occur 3–14 days after transfusion in patients previously sensitised to red cell antigens (e.g. Kidd, Rh), with extravascular haemolysis, positive DAT and new antibodies. They are usually mild but can be severe in sickle cell disease (hyperhaemolysis).
referenceText: Delaney et al. 2016 (transfusion reactions) [50]

stem: A patient with severe haemophilia A presents with a large muscle haematoma after trauma. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.A: Factor VIII concentrate, with haematology input
options.B: Fresh frozen plasma alone as the first choice

explanation: Factor VIII concentrate (recombinant or plasma-derived) is the treatment of choice in haemophilia A bleeding; dosing depends on bleed severity and target level. Patients with inhibitors need bypassing agents (rFVIIa or aPCC). Emicizumab prophylaxis affects some laboratory assays.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: A patient given topical benzocaine before bronchoscopy develops cyanosis and SpO2 of 85% that does not improve with oxygen; PaO2 is 200 mmHg. Co-oximetry shows methaemoglobin 32%. What is the treatment?
explanation: Methaemoglobinaemia causes "saturation gap" cyanosis with pulse oximetry often reading about 85% and normal PaO2. Methylene blue reduces methaemoglobin via NADPH-methaemoglobin reductase; it is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency, where exchange transfusion or ascorbic acid are alternatives.
referenceText: Nelson et al. 2019 (Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies) [151]

stem: Which statement about leucocyte-reduced red cell components is correct?

options.A: It eliminates the risk of TRALI
options.B: It prevents transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease in all recipients, like irradiation
options.C: It reduces febrile non-haemolytic reactions, HLA alloimmunisation and CMV transmission
options.D: It increases the risk of bacterial contamination
options.E: It is only used for plasma products

explanation: Universal leucoreduction reduces febrile non-haemolytic reactions, HLA alloimmunisation (platelet refractoriness) and transmission of cell-associated viruses such as CMV. It does not prevent TA-GVHD, which requires irradiation.
referenceText: Delaney et al. 2016 (transfusion reactions) [50]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: A haematology patient has a poor 1-hour post-transfusion platelet increment on two occasions despite ABO-compatible fresh platelets. No fever, sepsis or splenomegaly is present. What is the most likely cause and management?
explanation: Immune refractoriness, usually from anti-HLA class I antibodies, causes poor 1-hour increments. Non-immune causes (sepsis, DIC, fever, splenomegaly, drugs) more often reduce 24-hour survival. HLA-matched or crossmatch-compatible platelets improve increments.
referenceText: Kaufman et al. 2015 (AABB platelet transfusion) [111]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: What did the TRICC trial show in euvolaemic critically ill patients?

options.B: Liberal transfusion improved survival in all subgroups, including elderly patients and those with sepsis
options.C: A restrictive strategy (threshold 7 g/dL) was at least as effective as a liberal one (10 g/dL)
options.E: A restrictive strategy (haemoglobin 7 g/dL threshold, target 7–9) was at least as effective as a liberal strategy (threshold 10 g/dL)

explanation: TRICC found similar 30-day mortality with restrictive and liberal strategies, with lower mortality in younger and less severely ill patients receiving restrictive transfusion. It underpins restrictive thresholds in most critically ill adults.
referenceText: Hébert et al. 1999 (TRICC) [99]; Holst et al. 2014 (TRISS) [94]

stem: Why are viscoelastic tests useful in bleeding patients with cirrhosis?

options.A: They assess global clot formation, showing many with high INR have adequate haemostasis
options.B: They replace platelet counts and INR measurement in all patients with chronic liver disease

explanation: Conventional tests (INR, aPTT) measure only procoagulant factors and do not reflect the rebalanced haemostasis in cirrhosis. Viscoelastic testing evaluates clot initiation, strength and lysis, guiding targeted therapy and reducing blood product use.
referenceText: EASL 2018 (decompensated cirrhosis) [64]; Rossaint et al. 2023 (European trauma bleeding guideline, 6th ed.) [184]

stem: A patient taking rivaroxaban 4 hours ago presents with intracerebral haemorrhage. Which reversal agent is recommended where available?

options.B: Idarucizumab 5 g IV given as two consecutive boluses
options.D: Andexanet alfa, or four-factor PCC if unavailable

explanation: Andexanet alfa is a recombinant modified factor Xa decoy that binds factor Xa inhibitors; 4F-PCC (25–50 units/kg) is an alternative. Activated charcoal may be considered if ingestion was within 2–4 hours. Idarucizumab is specific to dabigatran.
referenceText: Tomaselli et al. 2020 (ACC oral anticoagulant bleeding pathway) [214]; Greenberg et al. 2022 (AHA/ASA intracerebral haemorrhage) [82]

stem: During a red cell transfusion, a patient's temperature rises from 37.0 to 38.3 °C without other symptoms or haemodynamic change. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Start broad-spectrum antibiotics and continue the same unit regardless of any further findings
options.D: Pause the transfusion, assess for haemolysis or sepsis, give paracetamol; resume only if safe

explanation: Febrile non-haemolytic reactions are common and caused by cytokines or recipient antibodies to donor leucocytes. Because fever can herald haemolytic or septic reactions, the transfusion is paused and the patient assessed. Leucoreduced components reduce incidence.
referenceText: Delaney et al. 2016 (transfusion reactions) [50]

stem: Which strategy is part of damage control resuscitation in a bleeding trauma patient without brain injury?

options.A: Routine use of recombinant factor VIIa
options.B: Permissive hypotension (SBP 80–90 mmHg) until bleeding is controlled
options.C: Aggressive crystalloid to normal BP before surgery
options.E: Delaying haemostatic products until laboratory results are available

explanation: European guidance recommends a target systolic BP of 80–90 mmHg (MAP 50–60) until major bleeding is controlled in patients without brain injury, limiting crystalloid, early blood products and haemostatic agents. In TBI, MAP of 80 mmHg or more is maintained.
referenceText: Rossaint et al. 2023 (European trauma bleeding guideline, 6th ed.) [184]; ACS Committee on Trauma 2018 (ATLS, 10th ed.) [5]

stem: A patient develops bloody diarrhoea followed by microangiopathic haemolysis, thrombocytopenia and AKI; stool tests detect Shiga toxin-producing E. coli. What is the mainstay of management?

options.D: Routine antibiotics to eradicate STEC and shorten the duration of toxin exposure
options.E: Supportive care, including dialysis if needed, avoiding antimotility agents

explanation: STEC-HUS is managed supportively; antibiotics may increase toxin release and HUS risk, and antimotility drugs are avoided. Plasma exchange or eculizumab may be considered for severe neurological involvement in adults.
referenceText: Zheng et al. 2020 (ISTH TTP treatment) [247]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: Which laboratory pattern best distinguishes DIC from thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura?

options.A: TTP is distinguished by a positive direct antiglobulin test
options.B: TTP shows low fibrinogen, whereas DIC shows normal fibrinogen with a normal D-dimer level
options.D: DIC: prolonged PT/aPTT, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer; TTP: usually normal clotting tests

explanation: DIC involves consumption of coagulation factors with prolonged clotting times, hypofibrinogenaemia and raised fibrin degradation products. TTP and other thrombotic microangiopathies have schistocytes and thrombocytopenia with typically normal coagulation tests, which helps differentiate them.
referenceText: Taylor et al. 2001 (ISTH overt DIC score) [206]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: An ICU patient develops a symptomatic DVT of the internal jugular and subclavian veins associated with a functioning, still-needed central venous catheter. What is the recommended management?

options.A: Remove the catheter immediately and withhold anticoagulation to avoid bleeding
options.B: Therapeutic anticoagulation, keeping the catheter if still needed and functional

explanation: Catheter-related upper-extremity DVT is treated with anticoagulation; a functioning catheter that is still required need not be removed. Anticoagulation usually continues for at least 3 months, or as long as the catheter remains in place.
referenceText: Kahn et al. 2012 (ACCP VTE prevention, non-surgical) [108]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]
